subtopics.title: US Strategic and Military Ties with Greenland
subtopics.summary: The United States seized temporary control of Greenland during the Second World War to stop Nazi Germany from exploiting the Danish colony. It proposed a $100 million purchase offer to Denmark in 1946 and formalised American military access through a 1951 defence agreement. Today the US maintains Pituffik Space Base, which helps monitor potential missile threats.
facts: The US seized temporary control of Greenland in World War II
The aim was to prevent Nazi Germany from exploiting the Danish colony after Denmark's occupation
In 1946 the US proposed a $100 million offer to Denmark for outright purchase of Greenland
The 1951 US-Denmark Defence Agreement formalised American military access to Greenland
Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, is maintained by the US
The base monitors potential missile threats from Russia, China and North Korea
Greenland hosts critical infrastructure for the US Ballistic Missile Early-Warning System
Greenland lies within the GIUK Gap, a key chokepoint for monitoring naval movements in the North Atlantic
Greenland's ground stations can track polar-orbiting satellites
Greenland enhances NATO's ability to monitor Russian activities in the Arctic and North Atlantic

subtopics.title: Great Power Competition and the EU Anti-Coercion Instrument
subtopics.summary: China labels itself a Near-Arctic State and invests in Arctic research, while Russia has heavily militarised its Arctic coastline and the US views Greenland as central to countering both. Denmark's firm stance highlights the tension between territorial sovereignty and the strategic ambitions of major powers. The EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument, nicknamed the Trade Bazooka, is primarily a deterrent tool against economic coercion.
facts: China labels itself a 'Near-Arctic State'
China is investing in Arctic research and infrastructure
Russia has heavily militarised its Arctic coastline
The US views Greenland as central to countering both China and Russia
Denmark takes a firm stance on sovereignty over Greenland
The EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument is nicknamed the 'Trade Bazooka'
The Anti-Coercion Instrument is primarily a deterrent tool with capacity for proportionate retaliation
The Anti-Coercion Instrument responds when a non-EU country seeks to coerce the EU through trade or investment measures
Its objectives are to deter economic coercion and protect the EU's strategic autonomy
A French President urged the EU to invoke the Anti-Coercion Instrument for the first time against US tariffs amid the Greenland dispute
